title: “Craving, monks, is a net that widens the wandering, it sticks; because of this craving, this world is destroyed, bound, tangled like a ball of…
content: “Craving, monks, is a net that widens the wandering, it sticks; because of this craving, this world is destroyed, bound, tangled like a ball of thread, like a tangled skein, like muñja grass and babaja reeds, unable to pass beyond the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower realm, saṃsāra.”

title: “Suppose, monks, a man is struck by a single arrow. They do not strike him with a second arrow. Thus, monks, that man experiences the…
content: “Suppose, monks, a man is struck by a single arrow. They do not strike him with a second arrow. Thus, monks, that man experiences the feeling of one arrow. So too, monks, a well-taught noble disciple, when touched by a painful feeling, does not sorrow, grieve, lament, beat his breast, or become distraught. He experiences one feeling — a bodily feeling, not a mental feeling. Touched by that painful feeling, he does not feel aversion. Because he does not feel aversion toward that painful feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling does not persist. Touched by that painful feeling, he does not delight in sensual pleasures. Why? Because, monks, the well-taught noble disciple knows an escape from painful feeling other than sensual pleasure. Not delighting in sensual pleasure, the underlying tendency to greed for pleasant feeling does not persist. He knows as it actually is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape regarding these feelings. Because he knows … the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling does not persist. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is not bound. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it as one who is not bound. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is not bound. This, monks, is called a well-taught noble disciple who is not bound by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is not bound by suffering.”

title: “Monks, form is impermanent, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has…
content: “Monks, form is impermanent, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has no regret for past form, does not delight in future form, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form. Feeling is impermanent … Perception is impermanent … Formations are impermanent … Consciousness is impermanent, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has no regret for past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.”

title: “And what, monks, is non-restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a…
content: “And what, monks, is non-restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms, praises them, and dwells with lust for them, then that monk, monks, should understand: ‘I have fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘falling away.’ … There are sounds cognizable by the ear … odors … tastes … touches … There are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those phenomena, praises them, and dwells with lust for them, then that monk should understand: ‘I have fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘falling away.’ Thus, monks, is non-restraint.”

title: Elder Lakuṇṭaka-Bhaddiya: “Outside the parks, At the Ambāṭaka woodland, In the forest with its groves, Having abandoned craving, the root of craving, Bhaddiya sits in…
content:
Elder Lakuṇṭaka-Bhaddiya:

“Outside the parks,
At the Ambāṭaka woodland,
In the forest with its groves,
Having abandoned craving, the root of craving,
Bhaddiya sits in meditation —
Blissful, happy.”

Some people delight
In drums, flutes, and cymbals.
But I, at the root of a tree,
Delight in the Buddha’s teaching.

If the Buddha grants a gift,
I receive that gift.
I bear mindfulness of the body,
Constantly in all realms.

Those who mock me for my body,
Or follow me for my voice —
They do not know me,
Driven by sensual desire.

Not knowing the inside,
Not seeing the outside —
Blocked on all sides, the fool
Is carried away by words.

Not knowing the inside,
But seeing the outside —
Seeing only the external fruit,
He too is carried away by words.

Knowing the inside with wisdom,
Seeing the outside as well —
Seeing without obstruction,
He is not carried away by words.

title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that leads to such great harm as heedlessness. Heedlessness, monks, leads to great harm.”
content: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that leads to such great harm as heedlessness. Heedlessness, monks, leads to great harm.”

title: “Monks, if there were no gratification in form, beings would not become attached to form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become attached…
content: “Monks, if there were no gratification in form, beings would not become attached to form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become attached to form. If there were no peril in form, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because there is peril in form, beings become disenchanted with form. And, monks, as long as beings do not directly know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, and the escape as escape in regard to these five aggregates of clinging, they have not, monks, escaped from this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, with its ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans; they are not free from it, not detached, not liberated, their minds are not at ease. But when they directly know these five aggregates … as they actually are, then they have escaped … their minds are at ease.”

title: “Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them,…
content: “Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them, then delight ceases. With the cessation of delight, lust ceases. With the cessation of lust, bondage ceases. Not being bound by the bondage of delight, Migajāla, that monk is called ‘one who dwells alone.’ Even if he lives in the midst of a village crowded with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, ascetics of other sects and their disciples — still he is called ‘one who dwells alone.’ Why? Because craving, the companion, has been abandoned by him. Therefore he is called ‘one who dwells alone.’”

title: “Monks, how does a monk practice the qualities befitting an ascetic? Here, monks, for a monk, when the mind of sensual desire exists, that sensual…
content: “Monks, how does a monk practice the qualities befitting an ascetic? Here, monks, for a monk, when the mind of sensual desire exists, that sensual desire is abandoned; when the mind of ill-will exists, that ill-will is abandoned; when the mind of anger exists, that anger is abandoned; when the mind of hostility … hypocrisy … spite … envy … stinginess … deceit … fraud … obstinacy … impetuosity … conceit … arrogance … vanity … heedlessness exists, that heedlessness is abandoned … Monks, I say that if he practices the qualities befitting an ascetic, he can abandon the defilements that are stains of an ascetic, blemishes of an ascetic, faults of an ascetic, leading to a plane of misery, to a bad destination, to the taking up of an evil realm. He sees himself cleansed of all those evil, unwholesome states and sees himself liberated. Because he sees himself cleansed of all those evil, unwholesome states and sees himself liberated, gladness arises; from gladness, joy; from joy, the body becomes tranquil; from bodily tranquility, he experiences ease; from ease, the mind becomes concentrated. I say that it is because of inner mental concentration that he practices the qualities befitting an ascetic.”

title: “Monks, for one whose greed is not abandoned, whose hatred is not abandoned, whose delusion is not abandoned — he is called one who is…
content:
“Monks, for one whose greed is not abandoned, whose hatred is not abandoned, whose delusion is not abandoned — he is called one who is bound by Māra, trapped in Māra’s snare, subject to the Evil One’s will.

But, monks, for one whose greed is abandoned, whose hatred is abandoned, whose delusion is abandoned — he is called one not bound by Māra, freed from Māra’s snare, not subject to the Evil One’s will.

One who has abandoned greed, hatred, and delusion,
Him they call one with a developed mind,
One who has become Brahmā, the Tathāgata, the Buddha,
The one who has overcome enmity and fear,
The one who has abandoned all — such a one is called thus.”
